hook: A water company must know the lowest level its reservoir will reach this month, not just a dip that looks low. A relative minimum answers "lower than nearby"; the company needs "lowest of all". On a closed interval there is a short, sure way to find it: list a few candidates and compare.

ideas: Candidates Test (closed interval method): for $f$ continuous on $[a, b]$, list the endpoints and the critical points in $(a, b)$, compute $f$ at each, and compare.
No derivative signs needed: just values. Show the table of candidates and values in your answer.
The absolute extrema can be at endpoints. A relative maximum can lose to an endpoint.
On a calculator problem, find critical points with the graph or solver, store them, and evaluate the model at each candidate.

misconception.wrong: "$f'$ changes from positive to negative at $x = c$, so $f(c)$ is the absolute maximum."
misconception.right: A sign change is a local argument: it only compares $f(c)$ with nearby values. For an absolute extremum on a closed interval, compare the values at the endpoints and every critical point. Chief readers see this lost point every year.

summary: On a closed interval, a continuous function has absolute extrema, and they sit at endpoints or critical points. The Candidates Test evaluates $f$ at each of those and compares. A sign change of $f'$ shows only a relative extremum; an absolute one needs the comparison.
